Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Elena, at seventy-four, carried the precision of her long career as a pharmacist in the careful way she held her hands in her lap, yet her eyes constantly scanned the room. The decision to seek help had been a long time coming, the culmination of nearly fifty years of a private, undeclared war. The initial event was a lifetime ago, during her first marriage. She remembers it not as a continuous story but in a series of stark, silent photographs in her mind. There is the image of the front door slamming shut with a force that shook the wall, the look on his face as he turned on her, his voice dripping with contempt as he mentioned her "weak, useless family." Then, the image of the floral pattern on the living room rug, seen from inches away. When these memories surface, which they do without warning, her body remembers most vividly. She feels the phantom pressure on her back and the unyielding hardness of the floorboards beneath her cheek, her limbs locked in the same position of helplessness she was in all those years ago. An intense, hot wave of shame always accompanies these moments, a feeling so potent it silences her.

In the decades since, Elena has constructed a life of meticulous control. Her body, however, has never forgotten the need for vigilance. Even in the quiet home she shares with her second husband, Carlos, a gentle and loving man, she feels perpetually tense, her shoulders tight and her muscles coiled as if ready for an impact. She has come to believe that safety is an illusion. Every night, she finds herself listening intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, her hearing so attuned to the creaks of the old house that she can barely sleep. The home she and Carlos have built together, filled with pictures of their children and grandchildren, does not feel like a sanctuary to her; it feels like the most crucial place to remain on guard.

To manage this internal state of high alert, Elena has, over many years, systematically walled off parts of herself. She learned early on to avoid any strong emotion, believing that feelings were dangerous doorways to the past. When Carlos tries to embrace her or share a moment of deep connection, she feels an instinctive recoil, a need to pull away before the closeness becomes overwhelming. This has created a painful, unspoken distance between them. She also avoids her own reflection, turning away from mirrors so she does not have to see the woman she has come to view as irrevocably weak. This avoidance extends outward; she has slowly withdrawn from friendships and community gatherings, the effort of maintaining a calm facade while her nervous system is screaming danger having become too exhausting. This withdrawal has cost her dearly, eroding the social fabric that once brought her joy and reinforcing a profound sense of having lost faith in the goodness of people and the world.

Her work at the local pharmacy, once a source of pride and identity, has become a minefield. Standing behind the counter, she feels exposed. A few weeks ago, a customer, making small talk while waiting for a prescription, commented cheerfully on his upcoming family reunion. The innocent words landed like a blow, instantly transporting Elena back. She felt the familiar shame rise and had to grip the counter to steady herself, her mind suddenly blank. In that moment, she was certain she was no longer capable of the simple human interactions her job demanded, that the competent, respected professional she had been for decades was gone forever.

It was an interaction with her granddaughter last month that finally broke through her defenses. The girl, bursting with excitement, had thrown her arms around Elena’s neck to tell her about a school play. The sudden, uninvited closeness and the talk of family triggered a full-body reenactment of the memory right there in her kitchen. The feeling of being pinned down was so real she gasped for air. Seeing the fear and confusion in her granddaughter’s eyes, Elena understood that the fortress she had built to protect herself had become a prison, isolating her from the very people she loved most. She is here now, terrified of what dredging up the past will entail, but holding onto the fragile hope that she might one day feel safe in her own body and truly present with her family.
